title: Friend Functions and Friend Classes
relevance: Interviewers probe whether candidates understand C++ access control, when friend is idiomatic (operators, iterators), and the non-mutual/non-transitive/non-inherited rules of friendship.

phases.goal: Establish what a friend is and that friendship is only granted by the class that owns the data.

must_hit.point: A friend is a function or class explicitly granted access to another class's private and protected members.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines friend as an access grant to private/protected members, not as membership in the class.

must_hit.point: Friendship is always granted by the class that holds the data; an outside entity cannot take it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Stresses one-way grant from inside the class definition, never unilateral self-declaration.

must_hit.point: A friend function is a free function (not a member) that has been granted access to the class's internals.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes friend free functions from member functions (no ClassName:: on the definition).

must_hit.point: Python has no direct equivalent to friend; access control relies on convention rather than compiler enforcement.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts C++ friend with Python naming conventions like underscore prefixes.

probes: What is a friend in C++, and who decides that friendship exists?

hints.1: Think about private and protected members and who can reach them.
hints.2: Friendship is declared inside the class that owns the data.
hints.3: A friend is an external function or class granted private/protected access by that class; outsiders cannot declare themselves friends.

phases.goal: Explain how friend functions and friend classes are declared and the three hard rules of friendship.

must_hit.point: To make a function a friend, place friend plus the function declaration inside the class; access modifiers do not affect friend declarations.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions friend declaration inside the class body and that public/private placement does not change the grant.

must_hit.point: Declaring a whole class as a friend gives every member function of that friend class access to the granting class's private and protected members.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says friend class means all of that class's members can touch the grantor's internals.

must_hit.point: Friendship is not mutual: if A declares B as a friend, B can access A's privates, but A cannot access B's unless B reciprocates.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses a one-way key analogy or A/B example showing no automatic reverse access.

must_hit.point: Friendship is not transitive: if A is a friend of B and B is a friend of C, A does not automatically get access to C.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects chain-of-friends access; each grant is explicit.

must_hit.point: Friendship is not inherited: a base class's friend does not automatically access a derived class's privates, and classes deriving from a friend do not inherit the friendship.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States clearly that neither direction of inheritance carries friendship.

probes: If class A declares B as a friend, what can B access—and can A access B? Is friendship transitive or inherited?

hints.1: Treat friendship like giving someone a key to your house.
hints.2: Cover three separate rules: mutual, transitive, and inherited.
hints.3: Not mutual, not transitive, not inherited—each relationship must be granted explicitly to the named function or class.

phases.goal: Clarify when friend is the right tool versus public accessors, especially for operators.

must_hit.point: Friend is commonly justified for overloading symmetric binary operators and stream insertion/extraction operators when a free function needs private data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names operator+, operator<<, or operator>> and explains why a free function may need friend access.

must_hit.point: operator<< must be a free function because the left operand is std::ostream, which you cannot modify to add a member for your type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains left-hand ostream forces a non-member, and friend if private state must be printed.

must_hit.point: Prefer asking when friend beats a public getter or setter rather than using friend as a general encapsulation bypass.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Frames friend as a deliberate, narrow grant versus exposing internals publicly.

probes: When would you use a friend function instead of a public getter for operator<< on a custom type?

hints.1: Consider who owns the left-hand operand of <<.
hints.2: You cannot add a member to std::ostream for your class.
hints.3: Implement operator<< as a free function, and declare it friend if it must print private members.

phases.goal: Apply friend to idiomatic patterns and answer the common encapsulation interview traps.

must_hit.point: The Container/Iterator pattern is a classic friend-class use: the iterator needs intimate access to container internals that stay hidden from the public.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes iterator needing pointers/links or internal structure via friend class Iterator.

must_hit.point: Friend does not break encapsulation because the grant must appear inside the class definition; the author retains control over who gets access.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects the trap: explicit grant inside the class is controlled access, not a unilateral breach.

must_hit.point: Friendship is strictly granted to the specific named class or function and does not pass down to derived classes.

probes: Does friend break encapsulation? Is friendship inherited?

hints.1: Ask who would have to write the friend declaration.
hints.2: Contrast an explicit grant inside the class with an outsider declaring itself a friend.
hints.3: No—friendship is granted only by the class author inside the definition, and it is not inherited by derived classes.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use friend when a free function must access private state—especially symmetric binary operators and stream operators—rather than widening the public API with getters/setters for every consumer.

tradeoffs.topic: member operator vs free friend operator<<
tradeoffs.strong_answer: operator<< cannot be a member of your type because the left operand is std::ostream; implement it as a free function and friend it only if it needs private data.

gotchas.trap: Saying friend breaks encapsulation because it exposes private members to outsiders.
gotchas.correction: Friendship must be granted inside the class definition, so the author retains control; C++ forbids an external entity from unilaterally declaring itself a friend.

gotchas.trap: Assuming friendship is mutual, transitive, or inherited.
gotchas.correction: Friendship is one-way, non-transitive, and not inherited—neither base-class friends nor derived-from-friend classes get automatic access.

gotchas.trap: Treating a friend function as a member function (calling it with ClassName:: or expecting this).
gotchas.correction: A friend function is a free function declared with friend inside the class; it is called like a normal function, not as a member.
